content:
1. SpaceX cadence: In 2023, Falcon 9 completed 96 orbital launches (including Starlink and non-Starlink missions); in 2024, the tally reached approximately 108–110 (exact public accounting varies slightly by source, but the ~100+ range is consistent); in 2025, the cadence is on track near 120+ launches, driven by Starlink rideshare and high-priority government missions. For 2026, a realistic projection is 120–140+ launches, with Starlink continuing to drive volume and national security missions (NRO, Space Force) filling the remainder. Booster reuse milestones include B1058 (first to 20+ reuses, retired after its 20th+ mission in 2024), B1062 (retired after exceeding 20 reuses in 2025), and B1067 (retired after high reuse count in 2025), with an ongoing shift to reflight intervals of ~30–60 days for selected boosters. Starship V2 (Ship 25/28 and variants) and V3 (Ship 30/31 class) are in development; Boca Chica remains the primary orbital test site, with Florida orbital infrastructure still in permitting/construction. Hot-staging (stage separation with propellant bleed-through) is planned to improve performance. With Ship 30+ class and full reusability, LEO payload mass potential exceeds 200+ metric tonnes per launch; however, early V2/V3 flights will likely operate at lower masses until reliability matures. By end-2026, a realistic operational cadence for Starship is 0–2 orbital test flights (success defined by achieving orbit and partial reentry), with no expectation of routine operational deployment for government payloads before 2027.

2. ULA Vulcan Centaur: The BE-4 engine supply from Blue Origin has faced schedule risks, but as of 2025 the engine is qualified and in production; Vulcan’s inaugural payloads (including government demonstration missions) occurred in 2024, with national security missions (NSSL) launching in 2024–2025. The USSF NSSL certification process is ongoing, with full certification expected to support operational missions by 2025–2026. Amazon’s Kuiper constellation has allocations on Vulcan, with initial launches in 2024–2025 and a planned cadence through the late 2020s. ULA is retiring Atlas V and Delta IV Heavy, with the last Atlas V launches scheduled in the 2024–2026 window, transitioning national security payloads to Vulcan.

3. New medium-lift entrants: Rocket Lab Neutron is under development with first flight targeted for no earlier than 2025, with operational cadence by 2027 contingent on successful tests and Wallops pad readiness; realistic 2027 cadence is likely a few flights per year. Blue Origin New Glenn (LC-36, Cape Canaveral) has faced delays; first orbital flight slipped to 2025, with operational cadence by 2026–2027 likely in the low single-digits per year. Relativity Space Terran R’s first flight is scheduled for no earlier than 2025, with operational cadence by 2027 if pad and engine qualification progress. Stoke Space Nova’s first flight is not expected before 2026, with operational cadence uncertain. Firefly Alpha achieved initial orbit in 2022; MLV (Medium Launch Vehicle) is in development with first flight targeted for 2025–2026, but operational cadence by 2027 remains limited. Across these, realistic 2027 operational cadence is modest (single-digit annual launches combined), with capacity for small-to-medium government payloads.

4. Europe: Ariane 6 has two variants: A62 (two P120C SRBs) and A64 (four P120C SRBs); P120C is shared with Vega C. Avio’s status post-Vega-C anomaly is under review, with investigations ongoing and no confirmed long-term production halt; however, the company remains active in the consortium. ESA’s Boost! program supports commercial alternatives, including Isar Aerospace Spectrum (Germany), RFA One (UK/Germany/Italy), MaiaSpace (Switzerland), and PLD Miura (Italy); none have flown as of 2025, with first flights anticipated in the 2026–2028 window. Ariane 6’s inaugural flight slipped to 2026, with operational cadence by 2027 likely 2–4 per year depending on demand and certification.

5. China launch: Long March 5B (crew/large payloads), 7A (geosynchronous), 8 (medium), and 8A (upgraded medium) are operational; 9 remains a paper rocket with no confirmed flight date. Commercial entrants include CASIC Kuaizhou (small-lift solid), iSpace Hyperbola (small-lift solid), LandSpace Zhuque-2 (methane/LOX, with Zhuque-3 in development), Galactic Energy Ceres-1 (solid), and Orienspace Gravity-1 (solid, medium-lift); flight cadences in 2024–2025 show 10–20+ launches annually across these vehicles, with 2026–2027 likely to maintain or increase tempo. Note: Export control and ITAR considerations will heavily constrain U.S. procurement of Chinese launch services.

6. Constellations: Starlink Gen 2 (V3) is deploying thousands of satellites with high launch cadence, prioritizing polar and mid-inclination planes; Gen 3/V3 iterations continue to refine throughput and latency. OneWeb (now under Eutelsat post-merger) is completing its first-generation constellation with planned replenishment missions. Project Kuiper is in early deployment, with initial launches planned for 2025–2026 and a full constellation build-out extending into the early 2030s; 2026–2029 cadence will ramp as Amazon fulfills its FCC commitments. Iridium NEXT is largely complete, with selective replenishment and hosted payloads. GPS III/IIIF, GLONASS-K2, and Beidou augmentation are ongoing modernization efforts, with Beidou fully deployed and GLONASS-K2 flights beginning in the mid-2020s. These constellations collectively drive the majority of launch demand across the vehicles described above.
